document.name: The Kinzie house, built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable

grade.why: Pictured: 7 of the pictures on the Images tab show it.

documented_range.note: THE KINZIE YEARS, BOTH ENDS INFERRED. It opens in the fall of 1804, when Currey has John Kinzie buy the house from Le Mai and arrive 'in the fall of that year' (currey_1912_story_of_old_fort_dearborn, ch. II); Moses and Kirkland give Le Mai 1796 where Currey gives 1797, and the Kinzies' arrival is put at 1803 elsewhere, so the opening is the later of the two readings and the house stands earlier than this phase says, under du Sable and Le Mai, in a form no picture shows. It covers 1 and 14 August 1812: Currey, 'The house escaped the general destruction at the time of the massacre'. It closes at the end of 1833: Currey says it 'was finally demolished in the early thirties', the 1857 engraving shows it about 1833, and data/exclusions.json kinzie_house rules it unoccupied and 'dilapidated beyond repair' from 1832 and gone by 1835, so it stands in no 1835 view.

placement.position_note: PLACED BY TWO STATEMENTS AND THE 1812 GROUND, NOT MEASURED. Wau-Bun: 'On the northern bank of the river, directly facing the fort'; Currey: 'near the present foot of Pine Street', facing south 'having the river directly in front'. So the house is centred on the flagstaff's easting (E +1152, the fort's seat in data/scenes/1812.json) and set back from the e1830_natural north bank, which stands at about N +305 there and reaches its level 1.5 m ground by N +318, far enough to leave the 'broad green space ... inclosed between it and the river' the same sentence gives: 18 m of green between the piazza and the bank top. The set-back is this record's own (docs/LIBERTIES.md L-kinzie-house-1812-2497).
placement.symbolic_location: The north bank of the river directly facing the first Fort Dearborn, near the later foot of Pine Street (N. Michigan Avenue) at Kinzie Street, the site of Pioneer Court; front wall at local N +336.0, centred on local E +1152.0, the easting of the fort's flagstaff; facing south. This record's origin is the footprint's north-east corner, which a 180-degree facing puts at the frame's (0, 0).

footprint.note: FORTY FEET BY TWENTY-TWO, CITED TO NOTHING HERE. Du Sable's bill of sale of 1800 to Jean La Lime is reported to give the house as 22 by 40 feet (Quaife, 'Property of Jean Baptiste Point Sable', Mississippi Valley Historical Review 15:1, 1928, pp. 89-96), but that article is not in this corpus and was not read, so the figure stands as a reconstruction and the article is named only as what would replace it. It agrees with what the sources here do say: Wau-Bun's 'long, low building ... a range of four or five rooms' and every picture's long front, about twice as long as it is deep. The long side runs along the river.

stories.note: Wau-Bun: 'a long, low building'. Both engravings draw one storey under the eaves with no dormer.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. About ten feet to the eave: the engravings draw the piazza's posts nearly the height of the wall, and a piazza roof needs headroom under a low eave.

construction.note: Moses and Kirkland vol.1p.30 (committed text lines4953–4955): 'The house was of squared logs, after the fashion of the very best of the frontier mansions of that day.' This attests the substrate, not an uncoated dark finish. T-2484 retains the squared-log fabric and states its whitewash separately as a reconstructed choice; no weatherboard cladding or installation date is invented.

roof_type.note: Both engravings draw a gable roof with its ridge along the river and its gables at the ends.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Read by eye off the two engravings' gable ends, which are drawn in perspective and give no measurable pitch.

loft.note: No occupied upper storey or dormer is established by the credited pictures. Sarony's small gable light is modelled explicitly under end_openings; it is not evidence of an occupied loft. The earlier note saying no picture drew a gable opening was superseded when T-2516 adopted that light.

chimneys.note: Both engravings draw two stacks rising through the ridge, not against the gables.

piazza.note: Wau-Bun ch. XVII describes 1831: 'a long, low building, with a piazza extending along its front'. Currey: Kinzie, after he bought it in 1804, 'repaired it, added a veranda'. Neither dates the veranda before August 1812; Lossing's view, which sets the house against the first fort, draws it, and that is the reading this phase takes.

piazza_depth_m.note: Unattested. Seven feet, about a third of the house's depth as the engravings draw it.

piazza_posts.note: The 1857 engraving draws six posts across the front; Lossing's are fewer and thicker at a smaller scale. Six, from the clearer picture.

piazza_rail.note: The 1857 engraving draws a rail with balusters between the posts, open at the door.

piazza_roof.note: THE MAIN ROOF CARRIED DOWN OVER THE PIAZZA AT A BREAK (T-2516). Lossing, the Cram plate and the Teich painting draw one plane from the ridge to the piazza's eave; the 1857 engraving draws a flatter roof below the main one. Sarony's lithograph of Juliette Kinzie's sketch, the one picture by a member of the household, and Eastman's 1820 engraving, the earliest, both draw the two together: the front slope breaks to a flatter pitch over the piazza, so seen from afar it is one plane run down to the posts and seen close it is a break. Built as that: a flatter plane rising from the piazza's plate until it meets the main slope above the front wall (generators/archetypes/log_dwelling.py _swept_piazza_roof). T-2497 had built the 1857 reading, a separate roof hung under the main eave.

piazza_plate_m.note: Read through Sarony's solved camera (data/reference_views/kinzie_house_1812/sarony_1912.json): the posts' heads stand 2.83-3.14 m over their feet, and the piazza's eave 2.88-3.24 m. The Cram plate's camera reads the same: every post about 1.7 times as tall as T-2497's 2.0 m posts. So the posts stand nearly the height of the 3.0 m wall, as wall_height_m's own note says the engravings draw them, and the plate is 2.95 m.

piazza_pitch_deg.note: Read through Sarony's camera: the piazza roof meets the front wall's line 3.56-3.93 m up and its eave stands 2.88-3.24 m, over the 2.35 m from the wall to the eave, which is 14-17 degrees. Fifteen, against the main roof's thirty; it meets the main slope 1.19 m inside the front wall, 3.83 m up.

chimney_ridge_at.note: Fractions of the ridge from its EAST end, which is the footprint frame's -x end at this record's 180-degree facing. The 1857 engraving puts one stack 0.45 of the ridge from the west gable and the other 0.93, by the east end; Lossing agrees on the middle one (0.4 from the west) and draws his second near the west gable (0.1). Three pictures of the four this ticket lists (the 1857 engraving, the Teich postcard at 0.43 and 0.81, the Cram plate's one stack at 0.93) put the second toward the east, so the 1857 engraving's places are built and Lossing's west stack is recorded in his match record as where the pictures disagree.

front_windows_per_side.note: The 1857 engraving draws two sash either side of the door under the piazza. Lossing's piazza is in shadow and shows none; Wau-Bun's 'range of four or five rooms' is a front long enough to light each from it.

window_w_m.note: Scaled off the 1857 engraving against the door beside them: about as wide as the door is half.

window_h_m.note: Scaled off the 1857 engraving: tall sash, about two-thirds of the door's height.

front_shutters.note: The 1857 engraving draws the sash bare, dark panes in plain casings, with no leaf beside any of them.

end_openings.note: THE ENDS ARE PIERCED (T-2516); +x is the west end at this record's 180-degree facing, and `at` runs from the back wall. WEST: Sarony draws a small light high in the gable, a window toward the back of the end wall and a door toward its front with a step before it; read through his camera the light stands 3.3-4.2 m up across 2.6-3.8 m of the end's 6.71 m, the window 1.1-2.4 m and the door 3.5-4.9 m from the back. The Teich painting draws the same light (a small square high in the west gable), and the 1857 engraving and the Cram plate draw something dark high in the gable and an upright pale mark low on the end wall where Sarony's light and door are. EAST: Eastman 1820, the earliest picture, draws two small windows side by side at the eave's height, at about 0.3 and 0.74 of the end from its front corner; built in the log wall with their heads just under the eave, since a light is in the wall or in the gable above it and not both. The west light, 3.35-4.15 m up, is in the gable, which the archetype closes with a board face flush with the rake. The window is set at Sarony's height, its centre 2.1 m up where the front's stand at 1.67 m; the window and door width take the front's prototypes and the lights the archetype's0.7by0.8m. T-2484 explicitly overrides the west door's clear height to2.50m via reconstructed end_door_height_m; its0.02m sill gives a2.52m head under the3.0m wall plate. None is a historical measured dimension.

log_finish.note: T-2484 visible completion: the household's Sarony plate draws the front pale and its gable light in shade; Currey's caption expressly covers1804–1813 as well as1816–1828. Eastman's1820 plate also draws the main house's gable light. These do not date a coating to August1812, so using the existing whitewash finish on both squared logs and chinking is reconstructed continuity, not an attested paint colour/date or an assertion of weatherboards. It replaces the previous unsupported assumption that every pale depiction necessarily showed a later cladding. The hewn-log relief remains. L-kinzie-house-completion-2484 records the choice.

end_door_height_m.note: T-2484 west-end door: the actual before comparison leaves the generic1.93m door's head about10pixels below Sarony's tall drawn doorway; the nearby end window's head is only a little above the door's. A2.50m clear opening, with its0.02m sill, follows that relative head line and corrects a greater-than0.3m visible miss. It is bounded by the retained3.0m wall, not a measured historical height. Width, horizontal station, front door and every other end opening remain unchanged. L-kinzie-house-completion-2484.

function.note: Built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, 'a native of San Domingo and a negro', an Indian trader who lived in it for over eighteen years (Currey). John Kinzie's family home and the base of his trade from 1804, 'the family mansion of my husband' in Wau-Bun.

occupants.value: John Kinzie's household, from 1804; absent from 1812 to 1816
occupants.note: Currey: it 'remained the residence of John Kinzie and his family until the time of his death, in 1828, except during the four years of his enforced absence, from 1812 to 1816.' Nobody is drawn (L1).

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE MARGIN IS ONLY 35 m, which is inside the working horizontal uncertainty of the georeference (about 20 m) doubled, so the grade drops a tier: the tract is right if the constructed line is, and nothing here proves the line to better than that. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

document.research_note: THE FIRST HOUSE AT CHICAGO (T-2497, piece 1 of T-2484). Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, a Black man from San Domingo and the first non-Native settler at Chicago, built it before 1779 and lived in it for over eighteen years; Le Mai bought it in 1796 or 1797; John Kinzie bought it in 1803 or 1804, the sources differ, repaired it, added the piazza and planted the poplars. It escaped the burning of August 1812 and was gone by the mid-1830s. This record is the house as the Kinzies had it, which is the only form any picture shows; the green, its fence and its trees are kinzie_house_1812_green and data/flora/plantings/kinzie_house_1812_trees.json. The pictures it is matched to are data/reference_views/kinzie_house_1812/: Lossing 1869 and the 1857 engraving (T-2497), the Cram atlas plate, the Teich postcard and the two 1820 views (T-2498). Sarony's lithograph of Juliette Kinzie's sketch, sarony_kinzie_residence_currey_1912_plate (reproduced by Kirkland as kirkland_1893_kinzie_mansion_1812_plate), is solved into sarony_1912 (T-2516) and governs where the pictures disagree: it settled the piazza's swept roof and its height and the pierced west end.
